conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m Dr. Patel, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into your own well-being while you’re settling into life with your baby. Over the next few minutes I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—the EPDS—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling since delivery. It’s simply ten questions about the past week; there are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past seven days: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?
I’ve had a hard time laughing. Sometimes my partner cracks a joke and I try to smile, but it feels forced. Nothing has really felt funny this week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… that doesn’t sound like me. Most days nothing feels funny at all, and when someone tries to joke I just can’t seem to laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but this week it’s like, “what’s the point?” I still do them, but it feels flat, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t get her to latch right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m failing her. Even when my partner says it’s normal, I still feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s too quiet or her breathing sounds different. I check her a dozen times an hour. I know people say new moms worry, but this feels bigger—like I can’t turn it off even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few times. Once, I was just folding laundry while she napped and suddenly my chest felt tight, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I was sure something terrible was about to happen. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky the rest of the evening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the next is due, plus the laundry and the bottles—if I sit down I’m already behind. Sometimes I look at the mess and just cry because I can’t see how I’ll ever catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get her down, but then my mind keeps spinning—worrying I missed something, replaying every little cry, thinking I’m not doing enough. It takes me ages to fall asleep, and when I do I’m up again at the slightest sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes… I feel sad most of the day. Everything feels heavy, like I’m carrying this weight in my chest that won’t lift. Sometimes I’ll just look at her and start crying because I’m scared I’ll never feel truly happy again.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a few times this week. Usually it’s when I’m already tired and something small tips me over—like dropping a pacifier on the floor or realizing I forgot to thaw the milk. I end up sitting on the couch with tears running down, feeling like I’m failing even at the little things.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I would never want to leave her. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression Screening Summary  
Date: [today]  Clinician: [name/credentials]  

**Symptom Highlights**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care; feelings of maternal inadequacy  
- Chronic anxiety with intrusive worries about infant safety; one acute panic episode  
- Sleep disruption driven by rumination rather than infant demands  
- Overwhelm and sense of inability to cope with routine tasks  

**Pattern**  
Responses map to DSM-5-TR criteria for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset (moderate severity) and co-occurring anxiety features.  

**Risk Factors**  
✓ Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day  
✓ Diminished interest/pleasure  
✓ Insomnia when infant sleeps  
✓ Psychomotor agitation (racing heart, repeated checking)  
✓ Fatigue and feelings of worthlessness/guilt  
✗ No self-harm ideation reported; protective factor present  

**Screening Observation**  
Patient endorses multiple symptoms above clinical threshold for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; denies suicidal thoughts. Recommends expedited referral for comprehensive evaluation and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
